newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Bank Austria's "Rambo Randa" wins showdown.
newsitem.headline: Bank Austria's "Rambo Randa" wins showdown.

text.p: Gerhard Randa, the debonair chief executive of Bank Austria, has a passion for Harley-Davidson motorbikes, jazz, soul -- and swallowing up the competition.

The 52-year old banker, known for his cloak and dagger way of doing business, pulled off his biggest coup on Sunday when he bought Vienna's venerable Creditanstalt bank to create a goliath in the Alpine republic's over-populated financial sector.

Randa, at the helm of Austria's top bank since April 1995, engineered the takeover of the government's 70 percent stake of ordinary voting shares in number two bank Creditanstalt far away from the media's glare.
Bank Austria jumped into the race for Creditanstalt at the very last minute -- just one month before the end of a six-year privatisation battle that threatened to topple the coalition government.

Four weeks before entering the fray, Randa publicly denied the bank had any ambitions to mount an attack on its chief rival. The chief executive, referred to as "Rambo Randa" by fellow bankers, on Sunday admitted the battle plan had been studied months before.
Bank Austria ensured it clinched the deal by offering by far the highest price -- some three billion schillings ($269 million) more than a rival bid from an international consortium.

Such tactics hark back to the Austria's last big banking takeover contest three years ago when Bank Austria jumped into the fray at the last minute and successfully offered the top price to buy savings bank GiroCredit.
Grey-haired, bespectacled Randa was born in Vienna and entered Austria's generally soporific banking industry in 1967 when he joined savings bank Zentralsparkasse.
Randa -- characterised in banking circles as a gentle and publicity-shy individual, yet never afraid to go for the kill in his business dealings -- joined the board of Creditanstalt in 1986.

There he worked under chief executive Guido Schmidt-Chiari, whose professional fate now depends on his former employee, before leaving the conservative stronghold in 1990 to join the social democrat stronghold Laenderbank.
As chief executive he lost no time in masterminding the merger of Zentralsparkasse and Laenderbank in 1991 to create Bank Austria, which ousted Creditanstalt as the nation's biggest bank.
Randa, who likes to call himself "first a banker and second a socialist", is also president of Vienna's bourse and sits on the supervisory board of numerous Austrian companies.
He is married with two children. ($1=11.15 Schilling)
